summary: Dexchlorpheniramine is the dextrorotatory, more active isomer of chlorpheniramine, a sedating first-generation alkylamine H1-antihistamine used to relieve symptoms of allergic rhinitis (hay fever), urticaria, and other allergic conditions such as itching, sneezing, runny nose, and watery eyes. Like other first-generation agents it crosses the blood-brain barrier to cause sedation and has anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, urinary retention, constipation), so it should be used cautiously in narrow-angle glaucoma, prostatic hypertrophy (BPH), and urinary retention, and it has additive CNS-depressant effects with alcohol, sedatives, and tranquilizers. No single-ingredient FDA prescribing information is available; dosing here is taken from standard pharmacology references (BNF/Martindale) rather than an FDA monograph.
indications: Allergic rhinitis (seasonal and perennial hay fever) - sneezing, rhinorrhea, nasal/throat itching, itchy watery eyes
Symptomatic relief of upper respiratory allergy symptoms (in combination cough/cold products)

moa: Dexchlorpheniramine is a competitive antagonist at peripheral and central histamine H1 receptors, the dextrorotatory enantiomer being the more active form. By blocking H1 receptors it reduces histamine-mediated vasodilation, increased capillary permeability, and stimulation of sensory nerves, relieving sneezing, rhinorrhea, itching, and urticaria. As a first-generation agent it crosses the blood-brain barrier (causing sedation) and has additional anticholinergic (antimuscarinic) activity.

absolute: Hypersensitivity to dexchlorpheniramine, chlorpheniramine, or other alkylamine antihistamines
relative: Prostatic hypertrophy (BPH) with risk of urinary retention
Concurrent MAO inhibitor therapy (potentiates anticholinergic effects)
Asthma or chronic respiratory disease with thick secretions
Stenosing peptic ulcer or pyloroduodenal obstruction
Elderly (greater sensitivity to CNS and anticholinergic effects)
monitor: Degree of sedation and impaired alertness
Anticholinergic effects (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention)

preg: There is limited specific data for dexchlorpheniramine in pregnancy. As with other first-generation antihistamines, it should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed and on professional advice. OTC labeling advises asking a health professional before use if pregnant or breast-feeding.
lact: First-generation antihistamines, including dexchlorpheniramine, may be excreted in breast milk and can cause irritability or drowsiness in the breastfed infant; they may also reduce milk supply. Breastfeeding is generally not recommended during use, or a non-sedating alternative should be considered; consult a health professional before use.
renal: There is no FDA-monograph dosage adjustment, as no single-ingredient prescribing information exists. By standard pharmacologic principles, use cautiously in significant renal impairment and consider reduced or less frequent dosing because of accumulation and increased CNS/anticholinergic effects.
hepatic: Dexchlorpheniramine is metabolized in the liver. No specific monograph adjustment exists; use cautiously in hepatic impairment and consider lower doses, watching for increased sedation.

major: MAO inhibitors - prolong and intensify anticholinergic effects; avoid concurrent use
Alcohol and other CNS depressants (opioids, benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics) - additive sedation and CNS depression
moderate: Other anticholinergics (tricyclic antidepressants, antiparkinson agents, antispasmodics) - additive antimuscarinic effects (dry mouth, urinary retention, confusion)
minor: May mask warning signs of ototoxicity from high-dose salicylates or other ototoxic drugs
interactions.food: May be taken with or without food; take with food or water if it causes stomach upset
interactions.alcohol: Avoid alcohol - additive CNS depression and pronounced drowsiness
interactions.diagnostics: Discontinue antihistamines several days before allergy skin testing, as they can suppress wheal-and-flare responses and cause false-negative results

serious: Marked CNS depression or, paradoxically, excitability (especially in children)
rare: Blood dyscrasias (e.g. agranulocytosis, thrombocytopenia) reported with chlorpheniramine-class antihistamines
emergency: Severe anticholinergic toxicity/overdose - agitation, hallucinations, seizures, hyperthermia, arrhythmias
Respiratory depression (especially in young children and overdose)

monitoring: Degree of sedation and ability to drive/operate machinery
Anticholinergic burden (dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention)
Signs of paradoxical excitation in children
Confusion, dizziness, and fall risk in the elderly
counsel: This medicine commonly causes drowsiness - do not drive or operate machinery until you know how it affects you

Dry mouth is common; sugar-free gum or sips of water can help

Store at room temperature, 20-25 C (68-77 F); keep tightly closed and away from moisture
pearls: SOURCING NOTE: No single-ingredient FDA prescribing information exists for dexchlorpheniramine (the openFDA hit is a combination cough syrup); dosing and PK here are drawn from standard pharmacology references (BNF / Martindale) rather than an FDA monograph
Dexchlorpheniramine is the dextrorotatory, more active isomer of chlorpheniramine - roughly twice as potent as the racemate, so doses are about half those of chlorpheniramine
First-generation agent: sedating and anticholinergic; second-generation antihistamines are preferred when sedation must be avoided
Use caution in narrow-angle glaucoma, BPH/urinary retention, and the elderly (anticholinergic load, falls, confusion)
Additive CNS depression with alcohol, opioids, benzodiazepines, and other sedatives
Stop antihistamines a few days before allergy skin testing to avoid false-negative results
missed: Take the missed dose as soon as you remember. If it is almost time for the next dose, skip the missed dose and resume your regular schedule - do not double up. Because this medicine is often taken only as needed for symptoms, simply take the next dose when symptoms warrant.
overdose: Overdose produces exaggerated antihistamine and anticholinergic effects: in adults, CNS depression with drowsiness, coma, and cardiorespiratory collapse; in children, paradoxical CNS stimulation with excitation, hallucinations, ataxia, and seizures. Other features include fixed dilated pupils, flushed dry skin, hyperthermia, dry mouth, and tachycardia. Management is supportive - protect the airway and support respiration, control seizures, and manage hyperthermia and arrhythmias. Activated charcoal may be considered for recent large ingestions; there is no specific antidote (physostigmine is reserved for severe anticholinergic toxicity under specialist guidance). Contact a Poison Control Center.
